questions.question: In which year did Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar lead the Mahad Satyagraha?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1927**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mahad Satyagraha was led by Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar in **1927** to fight for the rights of Dalits to access public water sources.
 
• The movement took place in Mahad, a town in the present-day Raigad district of Maharashtra.
 
• The primary objective was to allow Dalits to drink water from the Chavdar Tank, which was previously restricted to upper castes.
 
• It was a landmark event in the **Dalit rights movement** and highlighted the practice of untouchability in India.
 
• Ambedkar publicly burned the **Manusmriti** during the protest, symbolizing his rejection of caste-based discrimination.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Untouchability:** A social practice in India where certain communities, primarily Dalits, were ostracized and denied access to basic rights and resources.
 
• **Manusmriti:** An ancient Hindu legal text that endorsed caste-based discrimination, which Ambedkar burned as a symbolic act during the Mahad Satyagraha.
 
• **Dalit Rights Movement:** A series of protests and reforms led by leaders like Ambedkar to fight against caste-based oppression and secure equal rights for Dalits.
 
• **Chavdar Tank:** A public water tank in Mahad, Maharashtra, that became the focal point of the Mahad Satyagraha.
 
• **Impact of Mahad Satyagraha:** The movement was a turning point in India's social reform, challenging the caste system and advocating equality and justice.

questions.question: The Boilers Bill, 2024, introduced in Rajya Sabha on 8 August 2024, seeks to replace which previous Boilers Act?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Boilers Act, 1923**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Boilers Bill, 2024, introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 8 August 2024, seeks to replace the **Boilers Act, 1923**, which has been in place for over a century.
 
• The Boilers Act, 1923, regulated the operation, inspection, and certification of boilers used in industries to ensure safety and efficiency.
 
• The Bill aims to modernize boiler regulations, addressing advancements in technology, safety standards, and industrial practices.
 
• It incorporates stricter safety norms and compliance measures to prevent boiler-related accidents and enhance energy efficiency.
 
• This initiative is part of the government's broader agenda to reform outdated legislation and align industrial practices with global standards.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Boilers Act, 1923:**

 
 
• Enacted to regulate the safety of boilers in industries to prevent accidents caused by steam pressure.
 
• Mandated periodic inspections and certifications of boilers by authorized inspectors.
 
• Defined penalties for non-compliance with safety standards.
 
 
 
• **Boiler:**
 
 
• A boiler is a closed vessel used for generating steam or heating water under pressure, typically used in industries like power generation, textile, and manufacturing.
 
• Boiler safety is critical as failures can lead to catastrophic accidents, loss of life, and property damage.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Safety Reforms:**
 
 
• The modernization of boiler regulations is part of India’s focus on enhancing workplace safety and operational efficiency.
 
• It aligns with global standards such as ISO 16528 for boiler and pressure vessel safety.
 
 
 
• **Key Technological Advancements:**
 
 
• Modern boilers now incorporate advanced automation, monitoring systems, and energy-efficient designs to improve safety and performance.
 
• The new legislation is expected to mandate the adoption of such technologies in industrial boilers.

questions.question: What impact did the Green Revolution have on India's dependence on food imports?

options.text: No change in dependence on food imports

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Decreased dependence on food imports**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Green Revolution in India, initiated in the 1960s, led to a significant increase in agricultural productivity, especially in the production of wheat and rice.
 
• It introduced high-yield variety (HYV) seeds, modern irrigation techniques, and chemical fertilizers, enabling self-sufficiency in food production.
 
• By the late 1970s, India transitioned from a food-deficient country to a food surplus nation, reducing its reliance on food imports.
 
• The Green Revolution helped India achieve food security, especially during times of population growth and economic challenges.
 
• It also played a critical role in alleviating famines and ensuring the availability of staple foods domestically, lessening external dependence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **High-Yield Variety (HYV) Seeds:** These seeds were pivotal to the Green Revolution, offering higher productivity compared to traditional seeds, especially for crops like wheat and rice.
 
• **Role of Irrigation:** The expansion of irrigation infrastructure, such as canals and tube wells, ensured a consistent water supply, crucial for HYV seeds' success.
 
• **Fertilizers and Pesticides:** The increased use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides significantly boosted crop yields but also raised concerns about environmental impact.
 
• **Impact on Rural Economy:** While the Green Revolution increased incomes for many farmers, it also widened the gap between large and small landholders, leading to socio-economic disparities.
 
• **Food Security Achievements:** India’s improved agricultural output enabled the establishment of the Public Distribution System (PDS) and buffer stock management, ensuring food availability during crises.

questions.question: The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**9th December 1946**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Constituent Assembly of India met for the first time on **9th December 1946**, marking the beginning of the drafting process for India's Constitution.
 
• The meeting was held in the Constitution Hall (now known as the Central Hall of Parliament) in New Delhi.
 
• **Sachchidananda Sinha**, the oldest member of the Assembly, was appointed as the temporary President for the inaugural session.
 
• A total of **207 members** attended this first session out of 389 originally elected members, as representatives from Muslim League and princely states largely abstained.
 
• This date is considered pivotal in Indian history as it laid the foundation for the creation of the world's largest democracy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constituent Assembly:**

 
 
• It was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, sent by the British government to discuss the transfer of power.
 
• The Assembly had members from provinces and princely states, chosen via indirect elections.
 
• The main purpose of the Assembly was to draft the Constitution of India.
 
 
 
• **Drafting Committee:**
 
 
• The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, was formed on **29th August 1947**.
 
• The Constitution was adopted on **26th November 1949** and came into effect on **26th January 1950**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the First Session:**
 
 
• The first session set the tone for subsequent discussions and debates on the Constitution.
 
• It highlighted the challenges of uniting diverse interests, religions, and regions of India.
 
 
 
• **Constitution Hall:**
 
 
• The venue for the first session, the Constitution Hall, is now part of the Indian Parliament complex and symbolizes India’s journey to democracy.

questions.question: Which species of green algae, commonly known as stonewort, is often mistaken for a plant?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chara**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Chara** is a genus of green algae belonging to the Charophyta division and is commonly referred to as stonewort.
 
• It is often mistaken for a plant due to its complex morphology, including stem-like structures and whorls of branchlets.
 
• Chara is found predominantly in freshwater environments like ponds and lakes, where it grows submerged.
 
• Unlike vascular plants, Chara lacks true roots, stems, and leaves but has rhizoids for anchoring and nutrient absorption.
 
• Its body structure and reproductive mechanisms make it one of the closest relatives to land plants within the algal group.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charophytes:** A group of green algae that are the closest relatives to land plants, sharing similar cellular and reproductive structures.
 
• **Rhizoids:** Thread-like structures found in Chara that function similarly to roots, aiding in anchoring and nutrient absorption.
 
• **Stonewort:** The nickname "stonewort" comes from its calcified appearance due to the deposition of calcium carbonate on its surface.
 
• **Reproductive Structures:** Chara reproduces sexually using oogonia (female structures) and antheridia (male structures), which resemble plant reproductive organs.
 
• **Ecological Role:** Chara plays a vital role in aquatic ecosystems by oxygenating water, providing habitat for aquatic organisms, and stabilizing sediments.

questions.question: At room temperature and pressure, kinetic energy of the particles are minimum in case of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**iron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• At room temperature and pressure, the particles in solids like **iron** have the least kinetic energy compared to liquids or gases.
 
• In solids, particles are tightly packed in a fixed lattice structure, which restricts their movement, minimizing their kinetic energy.
 
• **Iron**, being a solid, exhibits strong intermolecular forces, which further limits the motion of its particles.
 
• In contrast, gases like methane and liquids like water or kerosene have particles with higher kinetic energy due to weaker intermolecular forces and greater freedom of movement.
 
• The kinetic energy of particles is directly proportional to their motion, and in the case of solids, this motion is minimal (restricted to vibrations about a fixed position).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kinetic Energy in States of Matter**

 
 
• Kinetic energy refers to the energy of motion. The particles in solids have the least kinetic energy, while gases have the highest.
 
• In liquids, particles have more kinetic energy than solids but less than gases, allowing them to flow but not expand indefinitely.
 
 
 
• **Intermolecular Forces**
 
 
• Solids like iron have the strongest intermolecular forces, keeping particles in fixed positions.
 
• Liquids and gases have weaker intermolecular forces, which result in greater freedom of movement for their particles.
 
 
 
• **Particle Movement in Solids**
 
 
• In solids, particles vibrate around fixed points but do not move freely, resulting in low kinetic energy.
 
• This is why solids maintain a definite shape and volume, unlike liquids and gases.
 
 
 
• **Temperature and Kinetic Energy**
 
 
• Kinetic energy increases with temperature as particles gain more thermal energy.
 
• At room temperature, solids like iron remain in their low-energy state due to their rigid structure.

questions.question: Which of the following classical dances is known to be ekaharya, where one dancer takes on many roles in a single performance?

__
 
• **Bharatanatyam**, one of the oldest classical dance forms in India, is known for its unique feature of **Ekaharya**, where a single dancer portrays multiple characters in a single performance.
 
• The term **Ekaharya** derives from Sanskrit, meaning "one actor" or "one character," highlighting the versatility of the performer.
 
• This dance form uses intricate **abhinaya (expressive gestures)** and body movements to depict multiple roles, often supported by rich mythological narratives.
 
• Bharatanatyam, originating from Tamil Nadu, is deeply rooted in **Natya Shastra**, an ancient treatise on performing arts written by sage Bharata.
 
• It is a highly codified art form performed in temples as a form of devotion and later evolved into a stage performance art.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Natya Shastra:**

 
 
• It is an ancient Indian treatise on performing arts attributed to sage Bharata, detailing various aspects of drama, dance, and music.
 
• It outlines the principles of Rasa (emotions), Abhinaya (expressions), and Mudras (gestures) used in Bharatanatyam.
 
 
 
• **Key Elements of Bharatanatyam:**
 
 
• **Nritta:** Pure dance movements without storytelling elements.
 
• **Nritya:** Expressive dance that conveys emotions and stories through gestures and facial expressions.
 
• **Natya:** Dramatic art, combining speech, music, and dance.
 
 
 
• **Ekaharya in Other Classical Dances:** While Bharatanatyam is prominent for Ekaharya, similar concepts can be seen in other forms like Kathak and Kuchipudi, though Bharatanatyam is most recognized for it.
 
• **Devadasi Tradition:** Historically, Bharatanatyam was performed by Devadasis (female temple dancers) as a form of devotion to deities in temples.
 
• **Modern Revival:** Bharatanatyam was revived and redefined as a stage art form in the 20th century by pioneers like Rukmini Devi Arundale.
